judge.rationale: Integrity holds: no clipped, overlapping or placeholder content on any of the ten pages, and every chart and table renders complete (slide 5's five-column table and slide 6's five-column comparison both fit their frames). Legibility is adequate but marginal in places — the body bullets on slides 2 and 10 are set far smaller than the slide scale warrants for a board room, and the axis/category labels on the slide 3 grouped bars and slide 8 stacked columns are the smallest type in the deck. Coherence is the deck's strength: the blue eyebrow label, blue conclusion title, and 'PAGE / 10 — CAPITAL ALLOCATION REVIEW — SEPTEMBER 2026' footer repeat identically on slides 2–10; the constraint cards on slide 7 are a clean 2x2 with matching rules; chart palette (blue/green/orange) is consistent across slides 3, 8. Only the green top rule on slide 1 sits outside the otherwise all-blue accent system. It fails at level 4 on communicative effectiveness. Slide 2, the executive summary, is three short bullets occupying the top third of an otherwise empty slide — the single most important page in a board deck is the emptiest; slide 10 ('What we're asking the board to approve') repeats the same three-bullets-then-void problem, and an approval ask deserves a structured, numbered decision block. No chart carries a source line: slide 3, slide 4, slide 8 and slide 9 all present figures with no provenance. Slide 4's bars are labelled 19, 11, 6, 14 with no percent sign anywhere on the plot, and slide 3's paired bars carry bare numbers where the axis is share of revenue vs share of capital. Slide 8's stacked columns have no takeaway caption despite being the recommendation page, and slide 3 buries its most important fact ('return on incremental capital ranges from 6% to 19%') in a 'Not shown' footnote rather than showing it. Titles are genuinely good — 'The highest-return division has the least room to grow', 'A return-only allocation would zero out Division C' — which is what keeps this from feeling anonymous, but the visual system itself (blue-on-white, eyebrow + statement title, rule-separated cards) is the default management-consulting shell and would carry any other subject unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, every slide has real content, and the footer ("Enterprise Fleet · Sept 2026" + n/10) repeats identically on slides 2–9. Coherence is genuinely good — the eyebrow label / conclusion-title / body pattern repeats without drift, the blue-green palette is consistent from cover (1) to closing (10), and the three chart slides (3, 5, 8) all use the same chart-left / three-annotation-right split, so nothing reads as hand-placed. Titles do the analytic work: slide 3 "Halyard took six points of share in two quarters", slide 7 "Option A protects the most value at the lowest margin cost", slide 9 "Run A and C together now; keep B on standby" are conclusions, not labels, and slide 7's table carries units on every column (Net 2-yr P&L impact, Margin impact in pt, Share @ Year 2 in %). Slide 10's four-row approval table with owner and date is exactly what a decide-this-month deck needs. What keeps it off level 5 and out of shipping unchanged: the slide 3 line chart is the smallest element on the busiest analytical slide — its axis ticks, the "Us"/"Halyard" legend and the y-axis label are set several points below the annotation text beside it, so the one chart that establishes the six-point loss is the least legible thing in the deck. None of the three charts carries a source line, so the share and P&L figures on 3, 5 and 8 are unattributed. Slide 9, the recommendation — the single most important page — is three short unstyled paragraphs floating in the top half with the entire lower third empty, which reads as unfinished next to the dense table on 7; the same emptiness appears under the A/B/C cards on slide 6, where the cards occupy barely half the frame. Slide 5's bar labels (160, 70, 78) also sit oddly against a $0–$120 axis, which invites a reader question the annotation doesn't answer. Not generic in content — the argument, the 22% breakeven and the named options are specific to this brief — but the container is a competent stock consulting frame that would look identical for any other decision deck."}

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text visible; slide 8's table rows and slide 9's continuation are deliberately split rather than overflowed, and the 'All five owners report progress...' note on 9 explains the break. Legibility is the first strain — the EBITDA chart on slide 2 has a y-axis label stack so small it is near-unreadable at deck scale, and its legend ('Northfield / Peer average') is smaller than any other type in the deck; slide 4's horizontal bar chart carries no value labels or axis units, so the reader must infer magnitude from bar length alone even though the adjacent table gives the exact EURm figures. Coherence is strong and consistently applied: the same eyebrow-caps/black-headline pattern runs from slide 2 through 11, tables share one rule weight and header treatment, and the black bookends (1 and 12) frame the deck. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns its level — titles are conclusions, not labels ('Procurement carries the largest share; four other workstreams complete the EUR 40m', 'Each owner carries two hard dates, not a general direction'), the governance org chart on 5 names every owner with their EURm number, and the cadence table on 6 has a purpose column. Gaps that hold it below 5: slide 2's chart has no source line under it and only a caption-style note; slide 3's '€40m' uses a euro glyph while every other slide writes 'EUR 40m'; the three date cards on slide 12 are visually identical grey blocks with no differentiation of the near-term commitment; and slide 7's three phase cards leave a large empty band beneath them, the one place the grid reads as under-filled. The italic 'Bring your team, bring the numbers, bring the pace.' on 12 is the only piece of styling that feels bolted on rather than designed. It is specific to this brief — real workstream names, real owners, real dates — not a template with blanks filled, though the underlying monochrome-with-rules system is a familiar consulting idiom.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text visible; every slide has real content and a consistent 'Customer Research Readout' footer. Legibility is the first real weakness — the body bullets on slides 5, 7 and 9 and the table rows on slide 10 are set at a very small size relative to the huge white margins around them, and slide 10's table text (esp. the 'Finding' column, '4.5 weeks actual vs 2 promised — top driver of early churn') is dense enough to be borderline at projection size; the chart axis labels on slides 4 and 8 are also very fine. Still readable, so it clears level 2. Visual coherence is solid and is where this deck lands: consistent eyebrow kicker in small caps italic, consistent title position and weight, consistent footer, repeated two-column chart+quote pattern on 4 and 8, repeated 01/02/03 numbering on 3, 6 and 11. It fails level 4 on several counts. Chart titles are absent: slide 4's bar chart has no takeaway label above it and its y-axis appears to be unlabeled/miscaled (values 2 and 5 plotted on an axis running to about 5, with no 'weeks' unit visible on the axis title), and slide 8's chart shows 40 and 11 on a 0–50% axis while the deck's numbers are percentages of lost-deal reasons — the unit relationship between bar height and label is not made explicit. Slide 8 has a source line ('Source: win-loss coding on closed-lost deals') but slide 4 has none, so source treatment is inconsistent. The two quote boxes (4 and 6) are labeled only 'Representative interview feedback' with no attribution or segment, weak evidence framing for a research readout. Slides 5, 7 and 9 are three consecutive all-text three-bullet slides with identical structure and a large empty lower half — the implication slides carry no visual differentiation from each other and waste roughly 40% of the frame. Slide 2's two stat blocks (34 / 1,200) sit in grey boxes but the supporting paragraph beneath is set at footnote size, inverting the emphasis relative to its importance. Genericness: the black-and-white, single-accent, Helvetica-ish treatment with italic eyebrow labels is competent but is exactly the neutral consulting shell that would look identical for a supply-chain or pricing deck; nothing in the visual language is specific to customer research — no interview/survey distinction in the chart styling, no sample-size or confidence treatment, no segment colour coding.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text is visible across the 15 tiles, and every slide carries a title, body and consistent footer/page-number. Legibility is the first real weakness — the bullet body copy on slides 2, 3, 6, 11, 13 and 15 is set extremely small relative to the slide width (bullets on 11 run to five near-identical lines of 8-ish pt grey text), and the chart annotations on slides 5, 8 and 9 are smaller again; on a projected committee deck those lines will not read from the back of the room. Coherence is the deck's strongest layer: title bar, hairline rule, footer 'Core Platform Modernization — Investment Committee' and page counter repeat exactly; the three KPI cards on slides 2, 3 and 15 use the same box treatment; tables on 6, 12 and 14 share the same header band and row rhythm. Where it stops short of level 4 is communicative effectiveness. Slide 4's bar chart of cumulative cost has no y-axis unit label visible (just '4, 8, 13, 17, 21' — millions? euros?), and slide 8's phased-cost bars are the same. Slide 5 plots 'Engineers' 5→2 as a line chart, which implies continuous decay of a headcount that actually steps — a column or waffle would be honest. Slide 9's crossover chart, the single most persuasive artefact in the deck, is a tiny two-series line with a legend so small the 'Replace' and 'Do nothing' labels are barely resolvable, and the crossover point itself is not annotated. No chart carries a source line. Slides 2 and 3 restate nearly the same four facts (14 years, EUR 4.2m, 3 of 5 engineers) with nearly identical KPI cards — a duplicated page in a 15-slide committee deck. Slide 7 is almost empty: four bullets and one italic line in the middle of a blank slide where a converging-timeline visual is clearly intended. Slide 10's phase blocks are the only piece of real composition and they use three arbitrary greys with the middle block near-black and its white type sitting on it inconsistently with the other two. Titles do mostly conclude ('Standing Still Costs EUR 4.2M a Year — and Compounds', 'Approve EUR 23M Now — the Window Is Closing'), which is genuine credit. On genericness: strip the words and this is an unstyled monochrome corporate shell — Arial-family type, grey rules, grey table headers, black bars — nothing about the mark, the palette or the layout is specific to this platform, this company or this decision.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text visible; the waterfall on p6 fits its frame, the p12 table fits, and the chapter dividers (3, 7, 11) render their numerals cleanly. Legibility is fine at deck scale — the black divider slides carry high-contrast white/grey type, and body text on 2, 13, 14 is set at a readable size with obvious left-to-right order. Coherence is strong and deliberate: the eyebrow rule + small-caps kicker recurs on every content slide (2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14), the page-number/left and 'GROWTH PLAN · BOARD READOUT' right footer is consistent, and the same big-figure-plus-right-column pattern repeats across 4, 5, 8, 9, 10. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns its level: the executive summary on p2 stands alone with three stat cards, three annotated sources and an explicit 'Ask' line; p6's bridge is a real waterfall with labelled steps (€218M → +€37.7M → +€31.3M → +€23.0M → €310M), a source-style footnote ('Figures in € millions. Darker accent = higher confidence'), and units on every number; titles are conclusions, not labels ('Confidence and investment trade off in opposite directions', 'How €92M closes: three sources, three levers'). The shared 41/34/25 share bar repeated on 8, 9, 10 with the active segment highlighted is a genuinely good device. What keeps it off level 5: the p6 waterfall is visually flat — the two mid bars are near-identical grey and the connector logic is hard to read at a glance, undercutting the deck's most important chart; the p12 table is small and unstyled relative to the confidence of the rest, with '—' rows in the Total line that read as unfinished; and p13's risk bullets use four differently-shaded squares whose meaning is never keyed. Genericness is low — the monochrome-with-one-accent system, the oversized 01/02/03 numerals on the dividers and the recurring share bar make this read as built for this specific three-source argument, not a filled-in template; it stops short of 0 only because the underlying grid is a fairly standard consulting title/eyebrow/two-column arrangement.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, no empty frames; the one blank cell bottom-left on slide 8 is just the 6/5 split of eleven projects. Legibility is fine at deck scale, though the body copy on slide 2 and the card text on slide 6 sit near the floor of comfortable reading. Coherence is strong and consistent — orange caps eyebrow, conclusion title, footer rule and page number repeat on every page, and the STOP/FUND/HOLD colour coding introduced on slide 6 carries through the eyebrows on 8/9/10 and the bubbles on 7. One repetition break: slide 8 carries a red vertical stripe at the left edge that slides 9 and 10 do not, so the decision trio does not repeat cleanly. Communicatively it is above average — titles are conclusions, not labels ('The board approved 50/30/20. The portfolio runs 78/15/7.', 'More than half of annual spend sits in projects earning nothing'), charts on 4 and 5 carry sources and footnotes, and every figure is unit-tagged (€m/yr, €m). What stops it short of 5 is composition on the pages that matter most. Slide 7, the named deliverable of the brief, renders the two-axis map as a plot occupying roughly the left two-thirds with a large dead band down the right side, and reduces 23 projects to three summary bubbles — the map asserts the segmentation rather than showing it, and the slide looks unbalanced next to the tightly-filled slide 6 that sets it up. Slides 9 and 10 leave a third to half the page empty below four- and eight-row tables, so the decision sequence loses rhythm exactly where 8 was dense. The tables on 8–10 are also thin: project name plus one number, twice across, which is a list formatted as a table. Not generic — the dark cover, the decision-coloured spine, the ambition-vs-actual pairing and the before/after reallocation on 11 are built for this argument, not dropped into a shell — but I would rebuild slide 7 and rebalance 9 and 10 before putting my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, every slide carries real content, and the three segment figures (EUR 180m/620m/95m, 14%/5%/31%, 70%/40%/85%) recur consistently across slides 2, 4, 5 and 6. Legibility is adequate but strained at the bottom of the type scale — the card body copy on slide 2 ("+14% growth · 70% capability overlap · 4 incumbents") and the criteria table's "What it measures" column on slide 3 are set at footnote size for content that is doing primary argumentative work, and slide 5's grouped bars have data labels so small they are near-unreadable. Coherence is strong: the green eyebrow label, the bold statement title, the italic source line and the "ADJACENT MARKET SCAN | 0X / 10" footer repeat identically on slides 2–10, and the blue/orange/green segment coding is applied consistently to the cards (2), the table header (4), and the chart bars (5, 6, 8). Communicative effectiveness is the deck's real strength — every chart title states a conclusion rather than a subject ("Segment B is three to six times larger than A or C", "Segment C scores highest — capability fit and growth outweigh raw scale"), each has a source line and a weighting footnote, and units are attached to every number. What keeps it below level 5 is craft: slide 9, the recommendation — the single most important page — is four short numbered lines occupying the top third with the entire lower half empty, so the payoff slide reads as the least designed one; slide 5 gives a grouped chart no y-axis and no gridline reference, forcing the reader onto the tiny value labels; and the palette is the default blue/orange/green trio, which collides semantically with the green used for eyebrow labels and the green "PRIORITIZE — ENTER FIRST" chip, so green means both "section marker" and "Segment C". I would also check slide 3: the four listed weights (20/20/30/20) appear not to sum to 100%, and slide 8's footnote states a different weighting set — an inconsistency in the screening logic that undermines the whole recommendation chain. Not shippable unchanged for those two reasons. Genericness: the numbers are specific but the containers are not — title slide with a coloured block, three-KPI card row, criteria table, two bar charts, three-card compare, numbered recommendation, three-phase timeline is a sequence that would render identically for a pricing review or a vendor evaluation with the text swapped.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, every page carries content. Legibility is the first real weakness — the option tables on pages 5, 6, 7 and especially the five-column comparison matrix on page 8 and the risk grid on page 10 are set at a size that is fine on a printed A4 handout but marginal for a projected executive-committee deck; the body cells on page 8 ('Medium-Low — builds on existing tools', '18-24 months') are the smallest type in the deck and sit in a table with no zebra or column emphasis to guide the eye. Coherence is broadly met: consistent kicker/title pattern ('WHERE WE ARE', 'THE DECISION', 'OPTION 1 OF 3'), page number and running footer on every page, the same headline figure treatment (€14m / €9m / €4m) on pages 5-7, and the same five criteria repeated. Where it slips below level 4 is communicative craft. Page 3's spectrum device is essentially empty — a horizontal line with three tick labels and no axis meaning beyond 'Low centralisation' at the left end, with the right end unlabelled, and it concedes its own emptiness with the line 'All three sit on this spectrum and are scored against the same five criteria on the pages that follow.' Page 9's bar chart is the deck's one quantitative comparison and it is mis-specified: it plots what appears to be negative and positive euro values on an unlabelled y-axis reading '-2, 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10' with no unit on the axis and no source line; the caption carries the takeaway but the chart itself does not state €m. Page 2's three-stat band gives '11', '€14m' and '0' where the '0' (group shared-service functions) is a rhetorical zero doing little work. Page 10's risk table uses 'Low / High / Medium-Low' colour-coded words but the same three-colour system never appears elsewhere in the deck, so it reads as a one-off. Page 11 is the strongest page — a genuine recommendation with a reason list and a boxed option card — but its bullet block and the box are vertically unbalanced, leaving a large empty band under the box. Genericness: the structure (title, context, framing spectrum, criteria, one page per option, side-by-side, chart, risk, recommendation, roadmap) is the default consulting operating-model skeleton, and the three-phase 'Mobilise / Consolidate / Scale & Decide' roadmap on page 12 with 'Months 1-3 / 4-9 / 10-18' is boilerplate that would survive unchanged in any other client's deck. The visual language — black text on white, thin rules, one grey bar fill, no accent colour, no logo — is neutral to the point of anonymous. It is competent and would be safe internally, but I would not send it to a client under my name without redoing page 3, adding units and a source to page 9, and enlarging the page 8 matrix.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholders, all twelve pages carry real content, and the footer rule/eyebrow/page-number system repeats faithfully. Legibility is acceptable though pushed hard on slides 8, 9 and 11 — the three-column change table (slide 8), the seven-role table (slide 9) and the risk/mitigation table (slide 11) all run at a size that reads on a laptop but will strain in a boardroom, and slide 9's rows have no separating rules so 'Regional VP, EMEA' and its consequence blur together. Coherence is the deck's strength: consistent serif headline, small-caps eyebrow, left-aligned body, and the same black accent bar used as a device on slides 5 and 6. Two coherence lapses: the footer numbering appears to break sequence (slide 6's page number does not read as 06), and slide 7 uses a centred three-number layout that appears nowhere else, leaving the lower two-thirds empty with only a small caption. Where it fails level 4: the only chart, slide 4's 'Same function, four times over' bar chart, plots 4/4/4/3 across Finance, HR, Delivery Ops, Sales Ops — a four-value comparison that a sentence would carry — and its y-axis runs to 4.5 in half-unit ticks for what are whole team counts, with no source line anywhere. Slide 5's headline figures 380 / 340 / 180 carry no unit: accounts, people or roles is unresolvable from the card text. Slide 3's 62% is the one stat that is properly qualified ('of our top 50 accounts span more than one region'). Titles are genuinely good — 'Geography made sense once. It doesn't anymore.' and 'Customers buy by segment. We're organised by geography.' state conclusions, not topics — which is why the chart and unit failures are the thing holding it at 3.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text visible across the ten pages, and the blocker cards on 4-6 fill their frames. Legibility is the first real problem. Slide 3's seven-row table sets item, workstream, owner, date and status in type that is markedly smaller than the body type used elsewhere, and slide 7's status table repeats it; slide 8's milestone-track labels ('Sep 8 / Content approval', 'Sep 12 / Works council decision') and its footnote sit at the smallest size in the deck, well below what survives a projected room. The donut on slide 2 also relies on segment labels rendered inside the arcs at very small size, and the red '6%' sliver label is the crux of the whole deck. Visual coherence is genuinely good: the green top rule, eyebrow-caps-plus-sentence-headline pattern, the WHAT'S BLOCKING IT / MITIGATION AND PATH TO GREEN two-column blocker structure repeated identically on 4, 5 and 6, and the consistent 'Project Anchor - Sep 2026' footer all repeat cleanly. Communicative effectiveness is where it stops short of 4. The headlines do conclude ('Readiness is on track — three blockers need attention before close', 'Payroll cutover for 340 transferring staff is not complete'), which is the strongest thing in the deck. But the donut on 2 carries no source and duplicates the 94/17/7 figures already stated in the giant numerals beside it — the chart adds nothing the number column does not; slide 3's table has a Status column that is pure red-fill BLOCKER/AT RISK chips with no severity or impact quantified; slide 8's timeline reduces six milestones to undifferentiated dots with no dependency shown, so it does not actually show a 'critical path' as the title claims. Slide 7's five-status table and slide 3's seven-row table overlap in content without a clear division of labour. Slide 10 closes with a date list and an email rather than a decision ask. The colour system is a plain green/amber/red RAG with a blue accent — safe, legible, and interchangeable with any integration-management deck; the flat red chips on 3 and 7 are the only forceful moment and they are heavy-handed. It reads as a competent consulting shell filled with this brief's content: the wording is specific, the composition is not.

Not shippable unchanged, chiefly for the table and timeline type sizes on 3, 7 and 8 and the redundant, sourceless donut on 2.

Integrity holds: no clipped or empty frames, no lorem, and the numbered dividers (5, 7, 11) render fully. Legibility is mostly fine at projection size, but the sub-labels inside the KPI cards on 8, 9 and 10 ('Growth tier · 38 seats × $149', 'Shipments optimized — below value band') are set several steps below the body size and the white-on-mid-grey third card ('$92,000 / yr', '$340,000 / yr', '$19,800 / yr') sits at the low end of comfortable contrast for a room with lights on. Coherence is strong and clearly systematised: the same eyebrow/title pair on every content page, the same three-card comparison on all three account slides, black full-bleed dividers with 01/02/03 in identical position, and a consistent italic footnote line under tables and charts. Communicative effectiveness is the deck's best quality — titles state conclusions rather than topics ('Cascade Freight is underpriced by $24K a year', 'Harbor's price hasn't moved in three years', 'Prairie Line pays more than it uses'), the agenda on 2 carries times and a facilitation note, the WTP chart on 12 labels every bar with its value and carries a takeaway line naming price as the #1 objection, the segment table on 13 gives n, stated range, realized price and headroom with a summary sentence, and 15 closes with owner/date accountability. What keeps it below the top band is craft in the data pages: the bar chart on 12 is the plainest possible treatment — flat grey bars, a full 0–100 axis with horizontal rules, a rotated axis title — and it floats small in a page that is mostly empty, so it looks like a default plot dropped in rather than composed; the grey 'value-based' card on 8/9/10 reads more like a placeholder swatch than a deliberate emphasis; and the two dense tables (3 and 13) run at a type size that will be hard to talk a room through. Not generic in content — every page is anchored to this client's accounts, tiers and survey — though the all-greyscale Helvetica system carries no brand signal of its own.

Integrity holds — no clipped text, no empty frames, no lorem — but the deck fails at level 3 because the charts are broken as visual objects, not just plain. Every bar chart (slides 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) renders as two flat horizontal bars, black over grey, with no axis labels, no value labels, and no baseline. On slide 4 the 'Actual' bar (61.4) is drawn shorter than 'Plan' (63.0) by a margin far larger than 2.5%, and on slide 5 the Margin chart shows Actual visibly *shorter* than Plan when 18.2% beat 17.5% — the geometry contradicts the title. Slide 3's four-up grid compounds this: four unlabelled bar pairs at thumbnail size carry no readable information, and the Headcount pair reads the same visual direction as the Margin pair despite one being a miss and one a beat. Chart legends ('Actual, Plan') sit in ~5pt type below each plot, below any projection-legible threshold. Beyond the charts, rhythm breaks: slides 4–7 all use a left-chart/right-bullets split, but the bullet column starts at a different vertical offset on slide 7 than on 4–6, and slide 9's two status cards are unequal in height with 'STOPPED' orphaned on its own line while 'SLIPPED' sits inline. Slide 11's two decision cards are also unequal widths for equal-weight content. Positives: the status chips on slide 8 (green/amber/red) are the one genuinely well-built element, the eyebrow/title/footer system is consistent across all twelve pages, and slide titles are assertive conclusions ('Margin beat plan by 0.7 points on cost discipline, not volume') rather than labels — that is the strongest thing here. But no chart carries a source line, and no chart has a stated takeaway inside the plot area; the takeaway lives only in the title. Slide 12 is nearly empty — a title, four lines, and 'Thank you.' floating mid-page. Genericness 3: apart from the status chips, this is the default black-on-white sans deck with a black title slide; swap the numbers and it would serve any business unit in any quarter.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text anywhere on the twelve pages; the NPS line chart (p3), the mechanism chain (p4) and the milestone timeline (p11) all render complete with axis labels and source lines. Legibility is adequate — the eyebrow/title/body hierarchy is consistent and the black-on-white palette carries contrast — though the annotation column on p3 ('Detractors now outnumber promoters...') and the axis text on the p5 benchmark chart sit at the small end of what a board will read on screen. Coherence is real: the eyebrow labels ('DIAGNOSIS · THE TREND', 'THE PLAN · PEOPLE'), the 'Customer Operations · Confidential' footer and the nn/12 page numbers repeat exactly, and the stat-card treatment on p2, p6 and p9 is the same object each time. Communicatively it is strong for the brief: titles conclude rather than label ('NPS fell 29 points in six quarters — and the fall accelerated', 'Two earlier fixes treated a symptom each — neither closed the loop'), the loop argument is made explicitly on p4, every chart carries a source and every figure a unit, and the p12 measures table ties baseline to 6- and 12-month targets with an explicit ask. What stops it at 4 and off the ship list: the three PEOPLE/PROCESS/TOOLING boxes on p8 are drawn full-height but their bullets stop a third of the way down, leaving three large empty rectangles that read as unfinished; p9 and p10 are bullet-only pages whose lower half is blank with no compensating device, breaking the visual rhythm the rest of the deck establishes; and the small bar pair on p5 (sector benchmark, 21 vs 44) is cramped against the 'Contact-centre turnover' card and reads as an afterthought rather than a designed comparison. Not generic in content — the loop diagram and the failed-attempts table on p7 are specific to this brief — but the eyebrow + conclusion-title + bullets + stat-card grammar is standard consulting-deck vocabulary that would transfer unchanged to any other turnaround story.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholder strings, and nothing overlaps on any of the twelve pages; the running footer 'SUPPLY CHAIN INVENTORY DIAGNOSTIC' and the x/12 pagination sit in the same place throughout. Coherence is genuinely good — the kicker/title/rule pattern repeats on pages 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 11, 12, the three dividers (4, 7, 9) share an identical ghost-numeral treatment, and the chart palette holds one black accent against greys everywhere (page 3 Current vs Benchmark, page 5 DC North/East, page 8 Current vs Target). Titles are conclusions, not labels: 'Inventory days run 57% above the 60-day benchmark' and 'Two of five distribution centers hold 61% of the EUR 41m' both state the finding. Where it fails the level-4 bar is density and evidence discipline. Page 2, the executive summary, carries three short bullet lines in the top third and leaves the entire lower half of the slide empty — the most load-bearing page in a diagnostic is the emptiest. Page 8 repeats the fault: four small bullets top-left, a small column chart top-right, and a large empty band across the bottom; the chart is also the smallest on the deck at roughly a quarter of the frame, so its axis values (61, 80) and its caption 'A 19-point gap to target' are set far below the type size of the body text elsewhere. Page 3's chart occupies barely the middle third and floats above a dead lower band. No chart on pages 3, 5, 6, 8 or 11 carries a source line, and only pages 3 and 8 carry an explicit takeaway caption — pages 5, 6 and 11 rely on the title alone. Page 11's rotated x-axis labels ('Current state', 'After intervention total', 'After redeployment 1/2/3', 'After forecast redesign SKU') are the smallest text in the deck and require the reader to tilt their head. Page 5's x-axis title reads as a cramped fragment about EUR millions of the 41m total rather than a clean unit label. The table on page 10 is the strongest page: ranked interventions, impact, difficulty, cash released, and a bold EUR 15.0m total row. Overall this is a clean, correctly assembled consulting deck that has not yet been composed — I would fix the empty lower halves on 2, 3 and 8, enlarge the page 8 and page 3 charts, and add sources before putting my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap, or placeholder text anywhere — slide 4's bar labels and slide 5's six-column lever table both fit their frames, and slide 2's donut sits clear of its legend. Legibility is fine at deck scale except the smallest tier: the body copy inside the four cards on slides 6 and 7 and the cell text in the decision table on slide 9 are near the floor of what reads from a room, and the orange footnote under the chart on slide 4 is the smallest live type in the deck. Coherence is strong and clearly systematic — the numbered eyebrow ('01 — WHERE WE STAND TODAY' through '09 — THE ASK'), the hairline rule at the top of every interior page, the footer 'DECARBONISATION ROADMAP · 2025-2030' with page number, and the dark-green bookends on 1 and 10 all repeat exactly; the two-card layout on 6 repeats faithfully on 7. Communicatively it does the job the brief asked for: titles conclude rather than label ('Scope 3 carries seven in ten tonnes of our footprint', 'Growth erodes the gains — a 4-point gap remains'), every figure carries a unit (84,000 tCO2e, €54/tCO2e, 18 pts), the donut on 2 is annotated with its boundary note ('2025 baseline · operational control boundary'), and the gap the brief demanded is named twice — as the orange footnote on 4 and as the '4 pts' hero on 8. Level 5 is not reached because composition is anchored to the top rather than composed: the lower half of slide 3 below the three-number row is empty, the two cards on 6 and 7 stop around the vertical midpoint leaving a wide void, and the tables on 5 and 9 end well above the footer. Colour discipline also slips on slide 4, where the bars run through sage, grey, three different greens and orange without the sequence reading as a deliberate encoding. Genericness is moderate: the deep-green/ochre palette and the numbered-section chrome are specific and consistent, and the content is unmistakably this brief, but the underlying page kit — stat triptych, card pair, plain table, two-column gap slide — is a standard consulting shell that would carry any other topic unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, overlap or placeholder text; page 3's table renders fully and page 4 ends cleanly with white space rather than a broken block. Legibility is the first real weakness — body type on pages 2 and 4 is set very small relative to the generous margins, and page 4's 'What would change this recommendation' bullets are the smallest text in the document despite being the analytically load-bearing section. Coherence largely holds: the running header ('Whitfield & Sons — Repositioning Assessment') and footer ('Confidential — Prepared for the Marketing Director') repeat on all four pages, and headings share one weight and scale. Level 4 fails on several counts. The three stat blocks on page 1 ('-4 pts', '38%', '61%') are stacked with no shared baseline or column structure and no source line — they read as three loose lines, not a metric row, and the up-arrow on 38% signals 'good' for what is a widening gap. There is not a single chart anywhere: a share-loss trajectory and a price-gap trend are the two obvious visuals the brief begs for, and their absence leaves page 2's option comparison entirely prose-bound. The page 3 table is the one genuine information design moment, but its column headers ('Option A — Narrow the price gap' / 'Option B — Premiumise') sit in a dark band that is the only dark element in the document and reads as imported. Headings are mostly descriptive rather than concluding — 'Two paths, two different businesses' and 'Immediate actions' state topic, not finding, though 'The problem is relevance, not price' and 'Recommendation: premiumise' do carry an argument. Page 4 has an orphaned continuation: numbered items 2-5 of the immediate actions float at the top of the page with no header, so the reader loses the thread across the break. Craft is unremarkable — near-uniform grey text on white, no accent colour tying the recommendation to anything, and the one-column stack could be lifted onto any category assessment by swapping the nouns; nothing here reads as built for a 90-year-old food brand specifically.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholders, no empty frames across the three pages. Legibility is the first real problem — page 1's opening paragraph under the H1 ('Fourteen months into a two-year...') and page 3's body text are set at a body size that is noticeably smaller than the page-1 stat callouts and reads as grey micro-type; more seriously, the page-3 recommendation paragraph and the 'If nothing changes' section are dense unbroken blocks with no numeric emphasis, so the single most important sentence in the brief (what the programme lands at if nothing changes — the 'EUR 30m' style figure) is buried mid-paragraph instead of surfaced. Visual coherence is broadly met: the dark-header table style repeats identically on page 1 (Workstream/Plan to date/Delivered/% of plan), page 2 (the 'Other workstreams / Total' continuation) and page 2's decisions table; the running head 'Cost Programme Review — Month 14' and the confidential footer repeat on all three pages. Where it slips to level 4 failure: the workstream table is split across pages 1 and 2 with the header row repeated but the 'Total 28.9 / 19.8 / 68%' row orphaned at the top of page 2, separated from the three rows it totals — the reader has to hold Procurement 118%, Property 41%, IT 33% across a page break to make sense of it. There is no chart anywhere: a three-workstream plan-vs-delivered comparison and a EUR 28m→19m gap are exactly the two things a bar or waterfall would land in one glance, and the document instead asks the reader to do arithmetic in a table. The page-1 stat trio (46 EURm / 19 EURm / 68%) is the strongest element and is well-labelled with units and captions, but 68% sits under a caption 'Of the EUR 28m plan to date — EUR 9.0m behind' that is doing more work than the number above it. The decisions table on page 2 does name owners (Chief Property Officer, Chief Information Officer, Programme Sponsor/COO) and dates, which satisfies the brief, but the 'Unlocks (EURm)' column values 2.5/1.5/0.5 sum to 4.5 against a stated 'half the shortfall' of a EUR 9m gap — the arithmetic visibly contradicts the framing, which is a communicative failure, not just a design one. Page 3 has no visual anchor at all: three headings and running prose on an otherwise empty page, with a large unused block at the bottom third. Genericness: the stat-trio and dark table header are competent but stock consulting-deck furniture; nothing in the type, colour or composition is specific to a cost programme or this client, and the same page-1 layout would serve any status review unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no overflow, no placeholder strings; the running header ("Meridian Fitness Group · Client Diagnosis") and footer ("Confidential — prepared for the leadership team · September 2026") repeat identically on all three pages. Legibility is fine — dark type on white, single column, obvious top-to-bottom reading order, and the two dark-header tables (p2 cohort retention, p3 revenue-at-stake) have adequate contrast in their header rows. Coherence is solid: the oversized-figure callout is a genuine repeated system — 5.9% ▲ +2.5 pts and 41% ▼ -27 pts on p1, 4 pts ▼ -23 pts closed on p2 — each with the same small caption underneath, and heading sizes/leading match across pages. Communicative effectiveness is met: the p2 cohort table carries a derivation footnote, the p3 revenue table ends in a $1.23M line plus a footnote converting it to ~$307k per quarter and explicitly framing it as not a worst case, units and signs are attached to nearly every figure (pts, %, $, months), and the two recommendations on p3 are numbered, named as actions (staffed onboarding at every site; promotional-rate-to-onboarding coupling) with a sequencing paragraph after them. Where it stops short of level 5: pages 2 and 3 both end roughly 40% short of the bottom margin, so the document reads as flowed rather than composed — the p2 break after "window the retention figures span" leaves a large dead band above the footer. The brief's central fact is a four-quarter trend from 3.4% to 5.9% and a cohort divergence, and neither is ever drawn — everything is prose plus two plain tables, so the reader assembles the trajectory mentally. Section headings ("What's actually happening", "What's already proven to work") are serviceable but state topic rather than conclusion, unlike the page-1 title which does. Visually it is entirely monochrome with no accent, rule weight variation, or brand signal; the callout figures are the only distinctive move, which is why it reads as a competent but interchangeable consulting memo shell around very specific content.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, no overlap on any of the four pages; the footer rule and 'Confidential — internal distribution planning use only' line and the 'Distribution Strategy Assessment' running head repeat identically on 1–4. Legibility is fine for a read-at-desk A4 memo, and the reading order is unambiguous. Coherence is good: the same table treatment (rule under header row, right-aligned numerics) is used for the channel table on p1, the channel-mix table on p2 and the investment-curve table on p2, and the bold lead-in paragraph pattern ('Segmentation.', 'Transparency.', 'Adverse selection.') on p3 is applied consistently. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns level 4: headings state conclusions rather than topics ('Why this is a funnel problem, not a pricing problem', 'The investment curve: when the shift pays for itself'), the p2 tables carry an explicit basis note ('Modelled on an assumed base of 50,000 new motor policies a year…') and every figure carries a unit (€96, €41, 14%, 2.1%, and the signed Net position column running −€1,442,500 → +€22,500 → +€287,500), and the brief's payback question is answered head-on by the oversized 'Year 2' display block on p3. It stops short of 5 on two specific defects. First, the p1 channel table breaks so that only the 'Other channels 13% n/a Aggregators; phone; not modelled' row lands at the top of p2 under a repeated header — a one-row orphan that a hand-set document would never allow. Second, p3 is rhythmically broken: a dense unbroken paragraph runs across the top, then the enormous 'Year 2' numeral with its single caption line consumes roughly a fifth of the page in near-empty space, and its message duplicates the sentence immediately above it. There are also no charts anywhere — the three-year net-position trajectory, the one thing the distribution lead will look for, exists only as a table on p2 while the sole visual gesture is a typographic numeral. Not generic: the p1 stat band (78% / 9% / €96 / €41 with labelled captions), the 'Other channels — not modelled' honesty row, and the payback numeral are all specific to this insurer's brief rather than slots in a shell. I would fix the table break and rebalance p3 before putting my name on it.

Integrity holds: no clipped or overlapping elements, no placeholder text, and the ESRS readiness table on page 3 fits its column widths with a Total row that reconciles (34/29/19 = 82). Legibility is fine at print size — dark text on white, single obvious column, headings numbered 1–8 in sequence. Coherence is mostly there: consistent heading weight, consistent bullet and numbered-list indentation, consistent body measure across pages 1–6.

Where it fails is level 4 and above. The page-2 statistic block ('34 datapoints / 29 datapoints / 19 datapoints') is the only display-scale element in the document and it is stranded at the top of page 2, orphaned from the section it belongs to — section 1 ends on page 1 and section 2 starts below the numbers, so the three figures float between two sections with no heading owning them. It is also the document's single most important fact and it appears before the reader has been told what the 82 total is. The ESRS table on page 3 has no source line and no units statement (they are counts, not percentages, but nothing says so), and the column head 'Collectable in year' is ambiguous about the fiscal year. Section 4, 'Scope 3 Emissions: The Critical Gap', is the analytically most important section in the brief and is delivered as three paragraphs of unbroken prose with no table of the 15 GHG Protocol categories, no marking of which are material, and no visual at all — the one place the reader needs a structured artefact gets the least structure. Section 7's list of what the report cannot say is well written but rendered identically to every other bullet list, so the document's most defensible content carries no distinguishing treatment. Page 5 also opens mid-sentence ('should use estimates deliberately and label them as such') with no visual continuation cue, and page 6 ends with roughly two-thirds of the page blank after the eight decisions.

Generically: apart from the one stat block, this is a Word-default memo — Calibri-ish sans headings, single column, no rule, no colour, no running header or footer, no page numbers visible, no client mark. A CSRD assessment for a manufacturer and a pricing memo for a SaaS firm would render identically. The subject matter is specific; the artefact is not.

Integrity holds on both pages: no clipping, no placeholder text, the payback table on page 2 is complete (Base case EUR 2.1m / Month 26 / ~2.2 years; Pessimistic EUR 2.1m / Month 34 / ~2.8 years) and the footer 'Confidential — Prepared for the Board' repeats. Legibility is fine — dark navy headings on white, generous leading, the three big stat figures (€340m, 9%, 61%) read at a glance with captions under each. Coherence largely holds: the same navy H2 rule-free headings, the same body measure, consistent numbered-condition list on page 2, and the dark navy table header band picks up the heading colour. Where it stops is level 4. The stat trio on page 1 is the only visual device in the whole document — the payback comparison, the single most decision-relevant content in the brief, is a plain three-column text table with no chart, no visual comparison of month 26 vs month 34, and no source line or 'as of' date on any figure. Section titles are labels, not conclusions: 'Market Opportunity', 'Entry Plan & Economics', 'Recommendation' say nothing, where the page-2 heading 'Conditions the Recommendation Depends On' shows the document could have done this throughout. The €340m/9%/61% row also carries no currency-basis or source note, and 'EUR 2.1m' recurs in body prose four times without ever being visualised against the 18-month spend curve. Page 2 is also visually thin — a table, a numbered list, a paragraph — with a large empty band at the foot, while page 1 is comparatively dense; the two pages do not share a rhythm. Genericness: the navy-on-white, big-number-trio, numbered-conditions structure is exactly what any market-entry memo would look like; swap Nordic hospital scheduling for any other sector and nothing about the composition would change. Nothing here is wrong, but I would not send it to a board with my name on it without a payback chart and titles that state the conclusion.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder text, tables on p2 (synergy tranche) and p4 (milestones) fit their columns, and the KPI trio on p1 (31% / 12 of 41 / EUR 8.2m per year) renders cleanly with units. Legibility is adequate: dark type on white, single column, obvious top-to-bottom reading order, though the running header 'Alderwood Facilities Group · Confidential' and the footer line are set very small and the body text on p3-p4 is at the low end for a printed committee read. Coherence is met: consistent section headings, one accent colour on the two table header bars, repeated header/footer on all five pages. It fails at level 4 on two counts. First, the page break economy is poor — p1 ends mid-sentence in Situation Assessment ('Overlapping depots mean duplicate property, management and dispatch cost that can be removed. Overlapping' runs off the page), and p5 carries a single short Recommendation paragraph on an otherwise empty page, so the deck ends on 80% whitespace. Second, and more damaging for this brief, the document is entirely prose and tables: the 60/40 synergy split, the four-phase sequence with its month ranges, and the deferral cost are all described in text and a milestone table but never drawn. A steering committee assessment about sequencing over 24 months has no timeline, no waterfall of the EUR 8.2m into the EUR 4.92m easy-win and EUR 3.28m migration-dependent tranches, and no chart carries a takeaway or source. The 'What a One-Year Deferral Costs' section on p4 is the sharpest content in the document — EUR 1.28m of annual run-rate, the 12 depots hostage, 31% of customers at risk — and it is buried in a plain bullet list at the bottom of a page rather than given the visual weight of the conclusion it is. Section titles are also topical rather than conclusive: 'Six-Month Milestones' and 'Recommended Integration Sequence' name the content, not the finding. Genericness is moderate: the phase names, the tranche table and the deferral arithmetic are specific to this deal, but the page furniture — small caps header, thin rule, centred confidential footer, one accent colour on table headers — is a generic corporate report shell that would look identical for any other subject.

Integrity holds across all four pages: no clipping, no overflow, no placeholder text; the page-2 three-tier table and the page-3 month/milestone table both wrap cleanly inside their columns, and the running header ("Harborline Parcel – Pricing Review") and italic confidentiality footer repeat on every page. Legibility is fine for a printed memo, though the page-2 tables are the weakest point — the "Rate action" and "Expected churn" columns compress to two- and three-word wraps ("+15–18%, 30-day 8–10% notice") at a noticeably smaller size than body copy. Coherence is strong: the KPI callout band repeats identically on page 1 (31% / 19% ▼ -12 pts / 22% ▲ / 0%) and page 3 (24.5% ▲ +5.5 pts / 93% / 94%), headings all sit under the same hairline rule, and both tables use the same dark header bar. Level 4 is met and then some: every heading is a conclusion rather than a label ("Two-thirds of the book is priced at or near a loss", "Sequencing by risk, not by ease, stops the worst accounts from bleeding in the fourth quarter", "If the two largest accounts refuse Tier 2 terms, the plan holds without them"), each table is followed by a plain-language reading of it, every figure carries a unit or a pts delta, and the page-4 numbered list closes on four dated decisions. Level 5 is not met on craft: page 1 breaks after the "Two-thirds…" heading and a two-line paragraph, leaving the bottom ~40% of the page empty while its supporting segment table starts fresh on page 2, and page 4 stops just past halfway with a large blank field. The one weak data point is the page-1 fourth stat, "0%" with a bare dash as its delta, which reads as an unfilled slot next to the three arrowed stats beside it. There is also no single visual — the entire argument runs on two tables and two stat bands — which is defensible for a memo but caps the distinctiveness. Genericness is moderate: the prose and numbers are unmistakably this brief (below-cost tier sizing, 9-month runway, the 34%-margin top accounts, the fuel-linked surcharge fallback), but the visual system is unaccented grayscale consulting-memo furniture that would carry any other subject unchanged.

Integrity mostly holds — no clipping or placeholder text — but page 5 is a hard failure of composition integrity: it carries only two orphaned numbered list items (4. and 5.) plus a two-sentence closing paragraph, leaving roughly 75% of the page empty above a footer stranded at the bottom. The 'Next 90 days' list on page 4 breaks across the page boundary mid-sequence, which is a pagination control that was never set. Legibility is fine at the intended print size: dark text on white, consistent serif/sans pairing, tables with dark header bands and readable rows. Visual coherence is largely met — the running header 'Procurement Savings Assessment' and 'Confidential — prepared for the Group CFO' footer repeat on every page, the table styling (dark header, alternating light rows, right-aligned figures) is identical on pages 3 and 4, and the KPI strip on page 1 (€96m / 340 / 68% / 40%) is echoed by the '75 of 340' and '40%' pair on page 2. Where it fails level 4: the page-2 stat pair sits in the middle of running prose with no rule or container tying it to the text, and the lone two-row 'Metric / Payback / Within Year 1' table pinned to the very top of page 2 is a fragment orphaned from the four-row metric table that ends page 1 — the same table split across a page break, with the header repeated but no continuation cue. The document is also entirely tables and prose: for a spend assessment with 68% concentration in eight categories, 22% of suppliers at 91% of spend and 40% price variance, there is not a single chart — no Pareto, no waterfall from gross addressable to net captured, no variance range by category. Section headings are descriptive rather than conclusive ('A fragmented spend base', 'What central contracting costs to run') where the analysis clearly supports assertive ones. Units are handled well (€m, % of total, FTE counts, wave numbers), and the three-year capture table on page 3 does carry gross/capture rate/net columns. Genericness is moderate: the numbers and category names (cleaning & housekeeping, laundry & linen, guest amenities) are specific to hospitality and the wave sequencing is real analysis, but the visual shell — plain black-on-white, no accent colour, stock KPI row, default table chrome — would look identical for any sector.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no empty frames, no placeholder strings across all seven pages. Legibility is mostly fine — the body serif is readable, the running header/footer are consistent, and the reading order is unambiguous single-column. Visual coherence is largely intact: consistent margins, consistent section-heading weight and size, the same dark-header table treatment on p2 (channel cost baseline), p4 (annual saving), p5 (transition investment) and p6-7 (roadmap), and the same footer rule everywhere. That earns level 3. It stops there for communicative reasons. The three KPI figures on p1 (EUR 1.34M / 44% / 3.9x) are the only non-text visual element in the entire document — seven pages of a cost-and-savings assessment with not a single chart. The 8%-of-contacts / 31%-of-cost asymmetry that is the analytical core of the brief is left as a sentence and a table row on p2 rather than shown. On p5 the '2.9 years' payback is typeset in a display size that collides visually with the section heading above it and sits orphaned between the investment table and the next H2 — it reads as hand-placed, not part of a system. The roadmap table splits across the p6/p7 boundary with the header row repeated but a row body ('upgrade national hubs') stranded alone at the top of p7. Table craft is weak: on p2 and p4 the numeric columns are not decimal-aligned and the currency column runs tight against the right rule; the p6 roadmap table has no visible column separation so 'Months 1-3' and the milestone text run together. Titles are mostly descriptive labels ('The Financial Case', 'Implementation Roadmap') rather than conclusions; only p1's title carries a claim. No chart takeaways or sources exist because there are no charts. Genericness: the accessibility section on p5 is genuinely brief-specific and well-observed (elderly passengers, disabilities, low-income, non-native speakers, complaints requiring documentary evidence), and the tier naming is particular to this service model. But the shell — centered serif title, thin rule, KPI triplet, dark-header tables, running header — would look identical for a hospital, a utility or a bank with the numbers swapped. Nothing in the typography, colour (there is effectively none beyond black and the table header fill) or composition says 'transport authority'.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap on any of the three pages; the header rule ('Store Portfolio Rationalisation - Property Committee Briefing') and footer ('Confidential — For Property Committee Use Only') repeat identically on all three. Legibility is acceptable but tight — the body measure on page 1 under 'The Closure List' runs to a very full line length at a small size, and the three captions under the stat trio ('Recommended for closure at lease expiry', 'Annual contribution recovered', 'Estimated sales transfer to the nearest sibling store') are set noticeably smaller and lighter than anything else in the document, close to the floor for a printed committee paper. Coherence is genuinely good: the segment table on page 2 and the Metric/Value table lower on the same page share one dark header treatment, heading weights and the italic deck under each H1 are consistent, and the bolded lead-in list on page 3 ('Path to breakeven', 'Catchment exclusivity', 'Sibling overlap', 'Online halo', 'Lease terms', 'Regional balance', 'Annual review') repeats one pattern cleanly. Communicative effectiveness mostly lands — the page 2 segment table splits the 62 contribution-negative stores into 18/21/23 with an explicit Disposition column, every figure carries a unit (€4.9m, 55%, 45%, 18 leases), and all three asks in the brief are answered. It falls short of level 5 on two counts. First, section titles label topics rather than state conclusions: 'The Closure List', 'Online Demand in the Affected Postcodes' and 'Criteria for the Remaining Leases' are agenda items, not findings, and the page 2 table is headed only 'Metric'/'Value' with no source or basis note for the 55/45 split — a property committee will ask where that estimate comes from. Second, the flow is unmanaged: page 2 stops roughly two-thirds down with a third of the page blank before the criteria section is pushed to page 3, and page 3 itself ends just past halfway, leaving a large blank block under 'Governance and Next Steps'. There is also no visual analysis at all — no distribution of contribution by store, no catchment map, no lease-expiry timeline — so the 3km sibling logic and the three-year expiry schedule stay entirely in prose. On genericness: the argument is specific to this brief, but the presentation system (grey-blue headings, three centred hero numbers, dark-header tables, bold-lead-in criteria list) is standard consulting chrome that would look identical for a supply-chain or pricing memo.

Integrity holds across all five pages: no clipping, no overflow, no placeholder text, and the running header (OPERATIONS BOARD BRIEFING) and footer (Confidential — Prepared for the Operations Board) repeat identically on every page. Body type on pages 3 and 4 is set at a comfortable measure with an obvious top-to-bottom reading order, and the section headings are editorial rather than generic — 'Where the Risk Concentrates' and 'The Economics of Acting Now' state a conclusion instead of naming a topic. Both tables carry units in the header row (Count / Share on page 3; Tier / Action / Timeline / Owner on page 4), and the recommendation is genuinely tiered into dual-source now, qualify over the year, accept and monitor, which is exactly the three-part ask. What stops it short of craft: the stat callout component is treated two different ways. On page 2 the three hero numbers (11, 35%, 19) sit stacked full width with a large, loose gap between each numeral and its grey caption, so the caption reads as floating rather than attached, and the captions wrap in a narrow column while the right two-thirds of the page stays empty — an executive summary page carrying roughly one short paragraph plus three numbers is under-dense for a board brief. On page 3 the same component is set as a tight two-up row (1.4% and 63%▼) with captions close underneath, which is the better treatment. The unit on page 2's first stat is run together as '11days' with no space or baseline separation, reading as a typesetting fault. On page 4 the tier table's first column is too narrow, breaking '1 — Dual-source' and '2 — Qualify' awkwardly against the wide Action column. Page 5 ends with roughly two-thirds of the page unmanaged white space below the four-line Conclusion. On genericness: the content is unmistakably written for this brief — the title 'Connectors, One Fire, and Eleven Lost Days', the 260/91/19 breakdown, the 1.4%-for-63% trade — but the container is a conventional single-column left-aligned Word memo with an eyebrow, a hairline rule and a stat stack that would carry any operations report unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipped tables, no placeholder text, no overlap; the three data tables (p3 headcount bridge, p4 hiring plan by level, p6 cost comparison) render fully with their dark header rows intact. Legibility is the first real weakness — body copy on pages 2, 5 and 7 sits at a very small size relative to a generous measure, and the tables on p4 and p6 use type noticeably smaller again than body text, so the numbers that matter most are the least readable elements in the document. Coherence is mostly held: the recurring header rule ('Workforce Plan – Prepared for the Managing Partners') and footer ('Confidential – Draft for Discussion') repeat on all seven pages, and heading levels are consistent. But the vertical rhythm breaks badly: page 1 stops around two-thirds down, page 2 has a large empty band under 'The Headcount Bridge, Year by Year' before the page ends, page 5 opens with an orphaned paragraph fragment then a wide gap before 'The Retention Plan', and page 7 is barely a third full. That gapping reads as flow accident, not composition, which is what caps this below level 4. Communicative effectiveness is uneven: the p1 KPI strip (+160 / 26% / 62% / £670k) is the strongest element in the document and does carry units and captions, and section titles like 'Recruiting Capacity — A Modest, Targeted Add' do conclude rather than label. But the brief's core artefact — the year-by-year headcount bridge — is a plain black-header table on p3 with no visual bridge, no chart anywhere in seven pages, and no source line under any table; the three-to-five-year 26% attrition cohort, the analytical heart of the brief, is argued only in prose. Distinctiveness is low: this is black text, black table headers, one hairline rule, and no accent colour or engineering-consultancy identity anywhere — swap the nouns and it is any firm's staffing memo.

Integrity is marginal and coherence clearly fails. Page 1 renders a bold "Contents" heading followed by empty space before "Executive Summary" — the TOC never populated, which is a visible blank placeholder on the cover page. Page 3 ends with the "Summary of Findings" heading and a dangling severity-table header row at the bottom margin, with the body of that table restarting on page 4; page 6 opens with the orphan cell fragment "is not programmatically indicated" floating above the "Serious — 14 issues" heading with no repeated header row, and page 10 opens with a stray "cycle" alone in the timeline column of the roll-up table. Repeated elements do not repeat consistently: some continuation pages get the black header band (p9 top), others do not (p6 top, p10 top). On page 4 only the "Serious" row is shaded cream in the severity summary while Blocker/Moderate are white, an arbitrary highlight with no key. Page rhythm is uncontrolled: page 3 is half empty under "Summary of Findings", page 12 stops a third of the way down leaving two-thirds white, while pages 5, 7 and 8 are jammed six-column tables where the Location/Remediation columns wrap to one or two words per line ("Payment — Add payment method.", "Yes — Form Field"), making them hard to scan at body size. On effectiveness: the report does carry the required content — WCAG SC column, shared-component column, effort in person-days, roll-up by severity and a phased retest schedule on page 11 — and the KPI band on page 2 (31/6/14/11) is a genuine attempt at a takeaway. But nothing is visualised: 31 issues across 3 severities, 22 journeys and 4 shared components are all delivered as monochrome tables with no chart, and the shared-component table on page 4 gives counts with no unit label beyond "Blocker instances". Typographically it is a plain black-rule-and-black-header-band report: no accent colour tied to severity (the one cream cell aside), no distinctive treatment of the blocker findings that are the report's whole argument. Clean enough to read, not something I would put my name on unchanged.

Integrity and legibility hold across all nine pages: type is comfortable, the red keyline and running header/footer repeat exactly, the dark-header tables on pages 4-6 are consistent, and nothing is clipped or overlapping. Two things stop it at visual coherence. First, the table of contents on page 2 runs dot leaders from every entry to the right margin with no page numbers at the end of any of them, so the leaders point at nothing — a TOC that cannot be used to navigate. Second, the vertical rhythm collapses: page 3 carries the entire Executive Summary in two short paragraphs with roughly three-quarters of the page blank; page 5 is an orphaned continuation of the plugin table (five rows, repeated header) with the rest of the page empty; pages 7 and 9 end at about 40% depth. The document is paced one section per page regardless of how much content the section has, so no two pages have the same text block depth and the grid reads as accidental rather than composed. Communicatively it is also thin where it matters most: the Executive Summary states that an evaluation is under way but never states the recommendation or the decision being asked for, and every section title is a label ("2. Current State", "3. Options Considered") rather than a conclusion. The 4,200 req/s, 180ms and 1.5 days/mo stat callouts on page 4 are the one strong moment — big numerals with unit labels beneath — but they appear once and are never used again, and there is no chart anywhere comparing self-hosted vs managed cost or latency, so the side-by-side comparison table on page 6 does all the analytical work alone.

Integrity mostly holds — no empty frames or placeholder text — but two cells break: on page 4 the Recommendations table header wraps mid-word as 'Prio rity' and a body cell reads 'Med um/ium' because that column is too narrow, and on page 1 the third KPI ('4.7× ▲ +37') orphans its unit 'min' onto its own line so its 'Over target' label sits a line lower than 'Current pipeline duration' and 'Target duration', breaking the three-up alignment. Legibility is otherwise fine: body type is comfortable at print size, the page-1 stat band reads first, and headings-then-prose ordering is unambiguous. Coherence is solid — the same running head 'CI Pipeline Performance Audit', the same 'Platform Engineering — Internal' footer, the same rule-under-heading and light table stroke on pages 2, 4 and 5. Communicatively it is competent: page 2's Measurements table gives time, share and note per stage with a 47 min total, page 3's headings are conclusions ('The dependency cache key does not match usage', 'Automatic retries mask the flaky-test rate') rather than labels, and page 5 pairs metrics with explicit targets. What holds it at 3 is rhythm and density: pages 2, 3 and 4 each stop around 55–60% of the page height leaving a half page of white below, page 1 leaves a full third empty under the executive summary, and there is not a single chart — the 19/14/9-minute split and the 6% flaky rate are given only as table rows, so the reader has to do the proportion work the brief was asking to see. Visually it is an unadorned all-grey text-and-rule report with no accent colour and no diagram; swap the words and it would serve a vendor review or a headcount memo unchanged.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, tables on pages 1–3 fit their columns, and the page 3 lever table's dark header row renders cleanly. Legibility is fine at document scale — the body serif is comfortable, the running header 'Capacity Forecast · Infrastructure Engineering' and 'Confidential — Internal Distribution' footer repeat on all four pages, and reading order is unambiguous single-column. Coherence is largely met: consistent margins, consistent heading weight, source lines set in the same small italic under both the page 2 forecast table and the page 1 demand table. Communicative effectiveness is where it earns level 4 — the page 2 assumptions list is explicit about the 2.7% month-over-month rate and the non-modelled categories, the page 3 lever table carries effect and primary risk per lever, units are attached throughout (vCPU-hours/month, TB, $/month), and the page 4 'Decision needed this quarter' section names an owner and a December 15 deadline. It stops short of level 5 on craft: the page 1 four-up stat band ('47% / 38% / 71% / 7') is the only display element in the entire document and is never echoed again, so the deck-style opener reads bolted onto an otherwise plain report; the caption under '7' — 'Months to committed capacity' — is also the weakest of the four, since a bare 7 next to three percentages invites misreading. More substantively, a brief this numeric produces zero charts: the twelve-month demand ramp on page 2 exists only as a four-column table (Month 3 / 7 / 10 / 12), and the month-seven breach — the single most important fact in the document — is asserted in prose on page 1 and again in a headroom row on page 2 rather than shown. Page 4's 'Move batch workloads to spot capacity' section is a wall of unbroken prose with no table, breaking the pattern the other two levers set on page 3. Genericness is moderate: the content is unmistakably specific to this brief (telemetry 90-day retention, 480 TB, $265,000/year, 262 TB one-time reduction), but the container — serif body, rule-under-heading, one dark-header table — would look identical for any other engineering memo. Not shipping unchanged: I would add a demand-vs-committed-capacity chart with the month-seven crossing marked, and give the spot-capacity lever the same table treatment as the other two.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, the seven-row retention table on page 3 fits its column widths, and the TOC on page 1 matches the section headings that follow. Legibility is fine — dark text on white, generous leading, an obvious single-column reading order, and a consistent 'Confidential — Internal Use Only' footer plus 'Data Retention Policy' running head on every page. Visual coherence mostly holds too: heading sizes step consistently (numbered H1 > H2 > bold run-in labels like 'Target Mechanism: Automated Lifecycle Management' on page 4 and 'Privacy position / Tax position / Resolution / Justification' on pages 5–6), and the dark-header table on page 3 with its alternating row banding is the one styled object and is styled cleanly. Where it falls short of level 4 is communicative effectiveness. The document is a wall of justified body text: pages 4, 5, 6 and 7 contain no visual structure at all — the deletion mechanism (section 4) describes an automated lifecycle with tag/purge-job/reconciliation stages entirely in prose where a small process table or stage list would carry it, and the audit trail (section 5) lists what each audit record contains as running sentences rather than a field table. The three conflict resolutions in 6.1–6.3 use a strong repeated four-move pattern (privacy position, tax position, resolution, justification) but never surface it as a comparison — the table on page 3 has a 'Conflict?' Yes/No column that flags exactly those three classes and then hands the reader to four pages of undifferentiated paragraphs with no cross-reference formatting. Section 3's table also mixes units in one column without a header note (30 days, 90 days, 1 year, 2 years, 7 years) and the trailing paragraph about trigger events and the 90-day deletion window is buried under the table rather than being a captioned note. Page 7's governance section is a single short paragraph occupying a whole page — a rhythm break with no compensating design. Genericness: the section skeleton, the Contents block, the plain black-and-white palette and the one dark-header table are exactly what any policy generator emits; nothing about the typography, colour, or page furniture signals this particular retention-versus-tax-code conflict as the document's spine, even though the brief makes that the hard part.

Integrity holds: no clipped or placeholder content across the three pages, the timeline table on p1 continues cleanly onto p2, and the remediation table breaks across p2/p3 without losing its header row. Legibility is adequate — the KPI row on p1 (1,842 / 214 / 19 min / 4h 00m) is the one strong typographic moment, and body text is readable, though the table body type on p2–p3 is noticeably small and the p2 timeline rows are dense grey-on-white. Coherence is mostly there: consistent running header 'Post-Incident Report' and 'Confidential — Internal Distribution Only' footer, consistent H2 treatment, but the KPI band's visual weight appears exactly once and never recurs, so p2 and p3 read as a different, plainer document than p1. Level 4 fails on several counts: the timeline table on p1/p2 has no unit label on the 'Elapsed' column (values read 'T+2:15m', '+15m', 'T+96m', 'T+8h00m' inconsistently — mixed formats within one column), the KPI '214' is labelled 'Orders duplicated (11.6%)' but the denominator is not stated at the KPI, and there is no chart anywhere despite a four-hour incident with a clean detection/diagnosis/resolution split that begs for a single timeline bar. Section titles are generic labels ('Summary', 'Impact', 'Timeline', 'Contributing Causes', 'Remediation') rather than conclusions; only the final heading, 'What Would Have Made This a Ten-Minute Incident', actually says something. The remediation table's 'Action' cells run long and wrap to four or five lines on p2, making the Owner and Target Date columns float in whitespace — the column widths were not tuned to the content. Genericness: this is a competent incident-report skeleton — left-aligned serif-ish headings, plain rules, a four-up KPI strip — that would look identical for a payments outage or a CDN incident with the words swapped. Nothing in the type, colour (there is essentially none) or page architecture is specific to this failover story.

Integrity holds: no clipped text, no placeholders, tables on pages 2–4 have complete rows and repeated header rows where they split, and the numbers from the brief (340 ms → 4.1 s, 200 → 500 pool, 2.4×/3.1×/3.2×) are all present. Legibility is fine — dark header rows on the run tables carry white type at adequate contrast, and the single-column flow gives an obvious reading order. Coherence mostly holds too: the running head 'Checkout Platform · Load Testing' and the 'Confidential — Internal Distribution Only' footer repeat on every page, and the three tables share one style. What blocks level 4 is page rhythm. Page 5 is a near-empty page carrying only three orphaned paragraphs of the Readiness Statement followed by roughly 85% white — a dangling last page that reads as uncontrolled flow, not a decision. Page 1 stops after the second Method paragraph with a third of the page blank before the footer, and page 3 leaves a comparable hole under the 'Bottleneck 2: Inventory Database Write-Lock Contention' paragraph. These gaps are not deliberate breathing room; they are the same body block ending wherever the break fell. Communicatively the document is otherwise solid — the page 1 stat trio (3.2× target / 2.4× current ceiling / 3.1× post-fix, with the +0.7× delta) states the conclusion up front, the NOT READY verdict is called explicitly, and the page 4 fixes table carries Status, Expected Ceiling and Effect columns with units on every figure. But there is no chart anywhere: the p99 degradation curve from 340 ms to 4.1 s across multipliers is the single most legible fact in this brief and it is left as table rows only. Styling is competent but unremarkable — black/grey table headers, no accent colour, no visual signal that this is a reliability report rather than any internal memo; the specificity lives entirely in the words, not the design.

Integrity holds on both pages: no clipped cells, no placeholder text, the Options Compared table on page 1 fits its column widths, and the 'Why Not A or B' section breaks cleanly across to page 2 without orphaning a heading. Legibility is fine — body text, the To/From/Date/Re block and the table cells are all comfortably sized for A4 print, and the only small type (the italic note under the table on page 1) is a secondary caption, not load-bearing. Coherence is consistent: the same running header ('Event Pipeline — Broker Selection', top right) and footer ('Memo — Engineering', bottom left) repeat on both pages, heading weight and the rule under the H1 are used the same way, and the salmon table header row is the only accent colour and it is used once. Communicatively it does the job well: the recommendation is stated in the first section rather than saved for the end, the table headers carry units ('Throughput (50k msg/s)', 'Monthly cost' with 'EUR 5,100'), and the page-2 heading 'What Would Change This Recommendation' answers the brief's explicit ask with four conditional bullets that name thresholds (30k ceiling, 50,000 msg/s, EUR 5,100/month). Two things keep it off level 5: the bottom ~45% of page 2 is empty with nothing composed into it, so the document ends by trailing off rather than closing, and the italic note under the table on page 1 is a run-on hedge that reads like a generated disclaimer rather than a deliberate table footnote. Nothing here is wrong enough to block sending it. On genericness: the prose is clearly written for this brief, but the visual treatment — plain memo header block, one tinted table header, one rule under the title — is the default memo shell; swap the words and it would look identical for a vendor selection, a postmortem, or a budget request.

Integrity holds: no clipping, no placeholder text, no overlap; pages 1–10 all render real content. Legibility is fine — the Section 3.1 field table on page 3 and the metric-name table on page 4 use small but readable type, and the running header/footer pair ("Observability Standard for Backend Services v1.0" / "Confidential — Internal Use · Platform Observability") repeats consistently. Coherence is met: the red rule under every numbered heading, the pink-tinted table header rows on pages 1/3/4/5/7, and the left-aligned single column repeat without drift. It stops at level 3 for two communicative failures.
